nameStory: Alpine Timothy gets its name from its mountain-loving nature - 'alpine' refers to its preference for high elevation habitats. It's also called 'alpine cat's-tail' because its cylindrical flower spike resembles a cat's fuzzy tail swishing in the mountain breeze.
description: Alpine Timothy is a hardy perennial grass that thrives in New England's highest elevations and coldest spots. This compact grass typically grows 6-20 inches tall, forming small clumps with narrow leaves and distinctive cylindrical flower spikes. Unlike its common cousin Timothy grass found in fields and lawns, Alpine Timothy is much shorter and stockier, built to withstand harsh mountain conditions. It's quite rare in New England, making any sighting a special discovery.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Dense, cylindrical spike 1-3 inches long that feels soft and fuzzy like a bottle brush, with a purplish-green color when fresh

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Low, compact clumps rarely exceeding 20 inches tall, much shorter and denser than common Timothy grass

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, flat blades that feel smooth on top but slightly rough underneath, with a bluish-green tint

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Found only in harsh, cold environments like mountain summits and exposed rocky areas where few other grasses survive

habitat: Alpine Timothy grows in New England's harshest environments - mountain summits, alpine zones, and exposed rocky areas above treeline. Look for it on Mount Washington and other high peaks of the White Mountains, often in areas with thin, rocky soil and extreme weather exposure. It may also appear in very cold, wet meadows at high elevations.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges late in spring due to harsh mountain conditions, appearing as small tufts of bluish-green leaves.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs in mid to late summer with the characteristic fuzzy, cylindrical spikes appearing purplish-green and soft to touch.
seasonality.fall: Flower spikes turn tan and become more papery, while leaves may take on golden tones before winter.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, leaving dried seed heads that may persist through early winter storms.

funFact: Alpine Timothy can survive temperatures that would kill most other grasses, including being frozen solid for months at a time - it's essentially nature's own freeze-dried grass that comes back to life each spring!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with common Timothy grass, but Alpine Timothy is much shorter (under 20 inches vs. 2-4 feet), grows only in harsh mountain environments rather than fields and roadsides, and has a more compact, clumping growth pattern. Remember: if you're not huffing and puffing from high elevation, it's probably not Alpine Timothy!
contextualKnowledge: With only 12 recorded observations in New England, Alpine Timothy is extremely rare and finding it represents a significant botanical discovery. Its scarcity is due to its very specific habitat requirements - it needs the harsh conditions that only exist at our highest elevations.
compareHints: Alpine Timothy differs from its common relative Timothy grass by being much shorter, more compact, and restricted to harsh mountain environments. While Timothy grass thrives in disturbed areas and farm fields at lower elevations, Alpine Timothy requires the extreme conditions of mountain summits and alpine zones. The flower spikes of Alpine Timothy are also proportionally shorter and denser than those of common Timothy.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Timothy differs from its mountain-dwelling relative Alpine Timothy by being much taller and having longer flower spikes.
